title: Mirror a 32-Bit Word
statement:
You get n, a 32-bit unsigned word, passed as a non-negative integer from 0 to 4 294 967 295 (232 − 1).

Reverse the order of its 32 bits: bit 0 swaps with bit 31, bit 1 with bit 30, and so on. All 32 positions count, including leading zeros. Return the result as an unsigned value in the same range, so a result with the top bit set is a number of 231 or more, never negative.

examples.why: 13 is 1101 with 28 zeros in front. Mirrored, its bits land at positions 31, 29 and 28: 2³¹ + 2²⁹ + 2²⁸. Reversing only the short string "1101" gives 11, which is wrong. And in JavaScript, forgetting >>> 0 returns −1342177280.
Only the top bit is set. Mirrored, only the bottom bit is.
Every bit is set except bit 0. Mirrored, every bit is set except bit 31.

hints: Build the answer one bit at a time. Which bit of n should become the top bit of the result?
Repeat 32 times: shift the result left by one, copy in n & 1, then shift n right by one. Leading zeros are handled because you always do all 32 steps.
In JavaScript, << and | produce signed 32-bit numbers. Finish with >>> 0 to read the same bits as unsigned. In Python, mask with & 0xFFFFFFFF whenever a left shift could push bits past position 31.

explain.intuition:
Think of the result as a stack: pop the lowest bit off n and push it onto the low end of result, shifting everything already there one place up. The first bit popped, bit 0, gets pushed up 31 times and ends at bit 31. Do exactly 32 rounds and every bit, leading zeros included, ends up mirrored.

The language detail is the real lesson. JavaScript's <<, | and & return signed 32-bit integers, so a result with bit 31 set comes out negative. x >>> 0 changes no bits; it just reinterprets them as unsigned. Python has the opposite problem. Its ints never overflow, so x << 16 on a 32-bit value can produce a 48-bit number. & 0xFFFFFFFF cuts it back to the low 32 bits, which is what fixed-width hardware does for free.
steps: Return result >>> 0 in TypeScript. In Python result already fits in 32 bits, since it was shifted only 31 times after the first bit went in.
pitfalls: Stopping when n becomes 0. The remaining zero bits still need to shift the result up. For n = 1 that would return 1 instead of 2147483648.
Returning a signed value in JavaScript. Without >>> 0, any result with bit 31 set comes out negative.
Reversing the binary string without padding it to 32 characters first.

solutions.title: Pad, reverse, parse
solutions.idea: Write n as exactly 32 binary digits, reverse the string and read it back in base 2.

solutions.title: Move bits one at a time
solutions.idea: 32 rounds: shift the result left, copy in the lowest bit of n, shift n right.

solutions.title: Swap ever larger blocks
solutions.idea: Swap neighbouring bits, then pairs, then 4-bit groups, then bytes, then the two 16-bit halves. Five masked swaps reverse the whole word. In Python, the final 16-bit swap needs & 0xFFFFFFFF.
solutions.ts:
function mirrorBits(n: number): number {
  n = (((n & 0xaaaaaaaa) >>> 1) | ((n & 0x55555555) << 1)) >>> 0; // swap neighbouring bits
  n = (((n & 0xcccccccc) >>> 2) | ((n & 0x33333333) << 2)) >>> 0; // swap pairs
  n = (((n & 0xf0f0f0f0) >>> 4) | ((n & 0x0f0f0f0f) << 4)) >>> 0; // swap 4-bit groups
  n = (((n & 0xff00ff00) >>> 8) | ((n & 0x00ff00ff) << 8)) >>> 0; // swap bytes
  return ((n >>> 16) | (n << 16)) >>> 0; // swap 16-bit halves
}
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def mirrorBits(self, n: int) -> int:
        M = 0xFFFFFFFF
        n = ((n & 0xAAAAAAAA) >> 1) | ((n & 0x55555555) << 1)
        n = ((n & 0xCCCCCCCC) >> 2) | ((n & 0x33333333) << 2)
        n = ((n & 0xF0F0F0F0) >> 4) | ((n & 0x0F0F0F0F) << 4)
        n = ((n & 0xFF00FF00) >> 8) | ((n & 0x00FF00FF) << 8)
        # n << 16 grows past 32 bits in Python, and no later mask cuts it back: do it here
        return ((n >> 16) | (n << 16)) & M
